lines.text: A notebook can be perfect for exploration and still be fragile as a recurring business process. Automation starts when the workflow has
explicit inputs, an entry point and predictable outputs.
Move a one-off notebook flow into a small script with pathlib paths, functions, explicit arguments and a main entry point. Prove that the
workflow works from a clean process.
Course 1 Python/pandas basics: variables, functions, DataFrames, read_csv and simple transformations.
5. New words before we use them
Entry point: The place where a script intentionally starts its workflow. Hidden state: Data or variables left behind by earlier notebook cells that later code
silently depends on. Deterministic run: A run that produces the same intended business result from the same approved inputs/configuration.
VISUAL/SOURCE ROUTE: Real Python short visual: file-path problem/pathlib overview; Corey Schafer 2024 pathlib is optional reinforcement.
After watching/opening: return to this lesson and reproduce the worked example from your own file/query/report. Save course-task evidence, not a screenshot of the
Clean-room runner: approved inputs enter a script through explicit paths/config, main() orchestrates small functions, outputs go to a defined
destination, and the same clean process can rerun without hidden notebook state.
Teacher demonstration - do this once with me, then close the example before your fresh task.
Use Path objects for input/output locations rather than hand-built string paths.
Create load_sales(path), clean_sales(df), validate_sales(df) and write_output(df,path). Each function gets what it needs through arguments.
Create main(input_path, output_path) that orchestrates the smaller functions.
Guard the command-line entry with if __name__ == '__main__': so importing the module does not unexpectedly run the business workflow.
Restart the Python process and run again. Then remove/rename the required input once to prove the error identifies the missing file before final
8. What you should see / be able to say
A clean-start script that can be rerun without notebook cell-order dependence.
Inputs and dependencies are visible in function signatures and main(), so the run no longer relies on invisible notebook memory. Professional upgrade: Use
configuration/arguments for paths and business period. Keep orchestration thin and transformation functions testable. A second analyst should know where
1. Copying the entire notebook into one long script. | 2. Hard-coding personal desktop paths inside cleaning logic. | 3. Using global DataFrames
that functions silently mutate. | 4. Writing final output before required-input validation passes.
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
12. Now you do a small version alone
Fresh case: refactor a customer-churn notebook into load_data(), normalize_status(), validate_data(), summarize(), write_output() and main().
Run from a clean process twice; input file unchanged; output row/total controls stable; missing input produces an actionable failure.
14. Teach it back in your own words
Explain why a script that works only after notebook cell 3 was run is not repeatable automation.
Save the first script and clean-run evidence before review. Changed retry uses a different input folder/output name through configuration only.
Script/notebook + clean-run proof + missing-input failure + rerun control + explain-back. After saving evidence, continue to PYA2.
One giant automation function is hard to test and risky to change. Small functions let you repair one behavior without breaking unrelated file
Design functions with one coherent responsibility, explicit parameters, useful return values, docstrings and lightweight deterministic assertions.
PYA1 script entry-point structure and basic function syntax.
5. New words before we use them
Function contract: Accepted inputs, returned outputs, assumptions and failure behavior. Pure transformation: A function that transforms supplied data without
hidden external side effects. Assertion: A check that stops or flags execution when an expected condition is false.
VISUAL/SOURCE ROUTE: Book-led; Python modules reference is sufficient.
After watching/opening: return to this lesson and reproduce the worked example from your own file/query/report. Save course-task evidence, not a screenshot of the
Function contract card: each function has one job, named inputs, a returned output, assumptions and an explicit failure rule. Small deterministic
checks prove the contract before the function is wired into the larger pipeline.
Teacher demonstration - do this once with me, then close the example before your fresh task.
Create normalize_channel(series) that returns a new normalized Series instead of changing a global DataFrame.
Create require_columns(df, required) that raises ValueError listing missing columns.
Create summarize_by_region(df) whose output grain is one row per region.
Add one normal assertion and one edge-case assertion to each critical helper where practical.
Keep file reading/writing outside pure transformations so tests do not need the whole filesystem.
8. What you should see / be able to say
Small composable functions with visible contracts and simple repeatable tests.
Each function can be tested in isolation with tiny deterministic inputs. Professional upgrade: Module boundaries matter more as analyst automation grows.
Keep transformations reusable and orchestration responsible for I/O and sequencing.
1. Function does discovery, cleaning, joins, charts and writes in one block. | 2. Returns nothing and mutates hidden global state. | 3. Catches its
own error and returns an empty DataFrame. | 4. Docstring says what code does but omits assumptions/failure behavior.
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
Circle each verb in the giant function. Each distinct responsibility is a candidate function boundary. Save the genuine attempt before review.
12. Now you do a small version alone
Fresh case: create normalize_priority(), validate_required_columns(), calculate_net_value() and summarize_team().
At least two assertions include a normal and edge/failure case; function outputs have stated grain.
14. Teach it back in your own words
Explain a function contract using input -> promise -> output/failure.
Attempt first. Changed retry adds a new channel alias without modifying file-loading/reporting functions.
Four functions + docstrings/contracts + assertions + explain-back. After saving evidence, continue to PYA3.
A pandas transformation can silently produce plausible values when dates/numbers were read as text or malformed records were coerced
away. Reliable automation treats dtypes and business calculations as contracts.
Parse dates/numerics deliberately, use explicit assignment under modern pandas behavior, calculate metrics vectorially and reconcile results
Course 1 pandas filtering/grouping and PYA2 functions.
5. New words before we use them
dtype contract: The expected data type for each important column. Vectorized operation: A pandas/NumPy-style column operation applied across rows
without manual Python loops. Coercion: Converting invalid values into another representation such as NaN/NaT rather than failing.
VISUAL/SOURCE ROUTE: Book-led with current pandas docs; IO video later reinforces file handling.
After watching/opening: return to this lesson and reproduce the worked example from your own file/query/report. Save course-task evidence, not a screenshot of the
Schema customs checkpoint: raw columns arrive at the border, required columns/types are inspected, invalid values are surfaced, transformations
happen only after admission, and independent row/amount controls prove that meaning survived.
Teacher demonstration - do this once with me, then close the example before your fresh task.
Load sales CSV and record raw row count.
Parse order_date with errors='raise'; parse quantity/unit_price/discount_pct as numeric with deliberate error policy.
Normalize channel using explicit assignment; avoid chained-assignment patterns.
Calculate gross_sales and calc_net_sales using vectorized columns.
Create validation_diff against supplied net_sales and fail/quarantine rows beyond the approved tolerance.
8. What you should see / be able to say
Typed DataFrame with explicit exception behavior and reconciled calculated metrics.
Bad types cannot silently flow through the same path as valid business records. Professional upgrade: pandas 3.x Copy-on-Write and evolving APIs make
explicit assignments and current documentation preferable to old notebook habits.
1. Leaving numeric fields as object/string. | 2. Using errors='coerce' without counting/quarantining new missing values. | 3. Chained assignment
on filtered slices. | 4. Checking only aggregate total while individual bad rows cancel each other.
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
Inspect dtypes and malformed examples first. Parse one critical column, count failures, then continue. Save the genuine attempt before review.
12. Now you do a small version alone
Fresh case: transform service transactions with mixed date/numeric formats and one malformed price.
No unexpected object dtype; bad-record policy visible; per-row reconciliation within tolerance; aggregate total reconciles.
14. Teach it back in your own words
Explain why 'pandas read the file successfully' is not a data-quality PASS.
Attempt first. Changed retry uses changed row order and one new malformed value.
Transformation function + dtype report + exception list + row/total reconciliation + explain-back. After saving evidence, continue to PYA4.
Manual copy/paste across monthly files is slow and unsafe. Automated discovery is only trustworthy when file scope, schema compatibility
Discover files with pathlib, sort deterministically, exclude backup/drift files deliberately, preserve source_file lineage and reconcile per-file
PYA1 pathlib/script structure and PYA3 pandas transformations.
5. New words before we use them
File-discovery contract: Rules defining which files are expected, included and excluded. Lineage: Evidence showing which source file produced each
row/output contribution. Schema drift: Unexpected change in column names/types/shape between files.
VISUAL/SOURCE ROUTE: Recommended visual: pathlib file discovery; use current docs for API behavior.
After watching/opening: return to this lesson and reproduce the worked example from your own file/query/report. Save course-task evidence, not a screenshot of the
File manifest conveyor: expected files are named first, discovery finds candidates, scope/schema checks admit only approved files, source_file
lineage is attached before concat, and per-file totals reconcile after combination.
Teacher demonstration - do this once with me, then close the example before your fresh task.
Use sorted(Path(input_dir).glob('sales_2026_*.csv')) but compare matches with an expected-file rule before loading.
Exclude files only through explicit contract, not because their values look strange.
Load each approved file, verify required columns, add source_file=file.name and record its row count.
Prove combined rows equal sum of per-file rows and produce a file contribution table.
8. What you should see / be able to say
One traceable combined dataset with deterministic file scope and schema checks.
Every combined row retains a source identity and file-level controls catch missing/extra contributions. Professional upgrade: File discovery, lineage and
schema checks are small-scale ingestion engineering patterns and transfer directly to DE work.
1. Glob pattern accidentally ingests backup files. | 2. Hard-coded list requires code edit every month. | 3. Concatenating incompatible schemas
and accepting NaN-filled new columns silently. | 4. Dropping source filename before validation.
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
Print expected vs actual filenames first. Do not read data until the file-scope mismatch is classified. Save the genuine attempt before review.
12. Now you do a small version alone
Fresh case: process four support-ticket exports where one backup and one schema-drift file are present.
Expected/actual file list, schema report, per-file rows and combined row parity all saved.
14. Teach it back in your own words
Explain why 'glob found 5 files' is not enough to know whether 5 files should be processed.
Attempt first. Changed retry switches to a new directory with a different approved month count.
Discovery function + file-scope table + schema checks + lineage + reconciliation + explain-back. After saving evidence, continue to PYA5.
Excel is a common analyst delivery format, but an attractive workbook can still contain wrong totals. Automation must treat the spreadsheet
as an output contract and verify it after writing.
Create a fresh Excel output from pandas results, preserve raw/template files, use deterministic sheet/column names and re-read exported
PYA3 transformations and basic Excel familiarity.
5. New words before we use them
Output contract: The required workbook/sheet/column structure and values expected by downstream users. Round-trip check: Writing an output, re-reading it
and reconciling against the source calculation. Template preservation: Keeping the provided raw/template workbook unchanged and producing a new output
VISUAL/SOURCE ROUTE: Corey Schafer pandas IO: CSV/Excel sections are useful visual support.
After watching/opening: return to this lesson and reproduce the worked example from your own file/query/report. Save course-task evidence, not a screenshot of the
Round-trip receipt: validated DataFrame -> new Excel output -> reopen the written file -> compare rows/columns/totals to the source calculation. A
successful write call is not evidence that the delivered workbook is correct.
Teacher demonstration - do this once with me, then close the example before your fresh task.
Build a validated regional summary DataFrame from the source truth.
Write a NEW workbook with a stable sheet name such as Regional Summary. Do not overwrite practice/template input.
Close the writer/process so the file is complete on disk.
Read the output sheet back with pandas.
Compare row count, region set and net-sales total to the source summary before declaring delivery PASS.
8. What you should see / be able to say
An Excel report whose saved values reconcile to the DataFrame that produced it.
The last-mile file is tested independently rather than trusted because writing did not raise an exception. Professional upgrade: For recurring delivery,
calculation truth should live in validated code/model logic; Excel is a controlled presentation/output surface.
1. Overwriting raw input/template. | 2. Hard-coded row numbers and manual formulas that break when regions change. | 3. No re-read after
export. | 4. Visual formatting used to distract from a failed total.
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
Strip to one output sheet and values only. Prove round-trip parity before adding presentation formatting. Save the genuine attempt before review.
12. Now you do a small version alone
Fresh case: create Team Summary and Exceptions sheets from support data and verify both after writing.
Template unchanged; expected sheets/columns; row and total parity; output opens after process ends.
14. Teach it back in your own words
Explain why successful to_excel() does not prove the workbook is correct.
Attempt first. Changed retry adds a new region/team without editing manual row formulas.
New xlsx output + round-trip checks + template hash/unchanged note + explain-back. After saving evidence, continue to PYA6.
CSV is flat, JSON may be nested, and careless normalization can multiply order-level values across item rows. File format handling is really
a grain problem plus encoding/schema discipline.
Read/write CSV/JSON safely, inspect nested structure, declare output row grain before normalization and reconcile nested item counts after
PYA3 pandas transforms and grain concepts from C2-00/C2-03.
5. New words before we use them
Nested JSON: JSON containing objects/lists inside other objects rather than one flat row structure. Normalization: Transforming nested records into a tabular
structure. Encoding: The character representation used when reading/writing text files such as UTF-8.
VISUAL/SOURCE ROUTE: Corey Schafer pandas IO: JSON sections; current Python json/pandas docs control syntax.
After watching/opening: return to this lesson and reproduce the worked example from your own file/query/report. Save course-task evidence, not a screenshot of the
Nested boxes to declared grain: inspect the CSV/JSON shape, decide what one output row represents, normalize only to that grain, then reconcile
parent/item counts so flattening does not multiply parent-level values.
Teacher demonstration - do this once with me, then close the example before your fresh task.
Load nested_orders.json with UTF-8 and inspect one order before flattening.
Declare output grain: one row per order item.
Use json_normalize/controlled list expansion to carry order_id and customer fields onto item rows.
Do not copy order_total into an item-level revenue measure unless its repeated meaning is intentional.
Count total nested items independently and reconcile to flattened row count; export deterministic columns.
8. What you should see / be able to say
Flat CSV/DataFrame whose row meaning and count exactly match the declared nested grain.
The grain is decided before flattening, preventing accidental double counting. Professional upgrade: Semi-structured data is common in APIs and event
systems; explicit grain and lineage are foundational pipeline habits.
1. Assuming JSON is already a table. | 2. Flattening one level too far/too shallow. | 3. Repeating order total on every item then summing it. | 4.
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
Draw one JSON object. Circle the repeating list. Decide whether one output row represents parent, child or combination before coding. Save the
12. Now you do a small version alone
Fresh case: flatten support cases containing a list of status events; preserve case/customer fields without overstating case-level SLA target.
Flattened row count equals nested event count; parent IDs retained; missing optional field handled explicitly.
14. Teach it back in your own words
Explain why JSON normalization is a row-grain decision, not just a pandas function call.
Attempt first. Changed retry removes one optional field from a record.
Normalization code + written grain + nested/flat count reconciliation + export + explain-back. After saving evidence, continue to PYA7.
Replacing a manual download with an API call can make a process faster but also introduces network failures, HTTP errors and changing
payloads. A weekly job must not hang forever or accept an error payload as successful data.
Explain request/response flow; write a defensive Requests wrapper with timeout, raise_for_status and bounded exception translation; keep
lesson mastery deterministic using local JSON.
PYA6 JSON handling and basic functions/exceptions.
5. New words before we use them
HTTP status: Numeric response status indicating request outcome such as success/client/server error. Timeout: Limit on how long a request waits for
network progress before raising an error. raise_for_status: Requests method that raises an HTTPError for unsuccessful HTTP status responses.
VISUAL/SOURCE ROUTE: Corey Schafer Requests tutorial is visual support; current Requests docs govern reliability.
After watching/opening: return to this lesson and reproduce the worked example from your own file/query/report. Save course-task evidence, not a screenshot of the
Courier request-response contract: client sends URL/parameters with a timeout, server returns status/body, raise_for_status and payload/schema
checks decide acceptance, and bounded exceptions distinguish network failure from valid empty data.
Teacher demonstration - do this once with me, then close the example before your fresh task.
First parse the supplied local api_response.json so network availability cannot block mastery.
Define fetch_json(url, timeout=15). Always pass an explicit timeout.
Translate Timeout and RequestException with useful URL/context while preserving the original exception chain.
Do not embed API keys/tokens in notebook/source evidence; use environment/config secret mechanisms in real work.
8. What you should see / be able to say
A wrapper whose success and failure paths are explicit plus a network-independent parsing exercise.
Transport success, HTTP success and JSON parsing are treated as separate conditions. Professional upgrade: Requests documentation explicitly
recommends timeouts for production code; reliability belongs in the wrapper, not every downstream parser.
1. requests.get(url) with no timeout. | 2. Calling .json() and assuming HTTP success. | 3. except Exception: return {}. | 4. Hard-coding credentials
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
Test parsing with local JSON first. Then test wrapper using a harmless endpoint only if network is available. Inject a fake/bad status or mock/local
failure path. Save the genuine attempt before review.
12. Now you do a small version alone
Fresh case: design a wrapper for a customer-status API and a parser that extracts one row per customer status record.
Local practice passes offline; timeout specified; HTTP failures cannot become valid data; credentials absent.
14. Teach it back in your own words
Explain why valid JSON can still represent a failed API response.
Attempt first. Changed retry changes endpoint/base URL through config only.
Wrapper + local parser + error-path evidence + security note + explain-back. After saving evidence, continue to PYA8.
PYA8 - Error handling and defensive scripts
The most dangerous automation failure is not always a crash; it is a script that swallows an error and publishes a plausible but wrong report.
Catch specific exceptions you can contextualize/recover from, re-raise with context, distinguish data-quality failure from technical failure and
block final output when trust controls fail.
5. New words before we use them
Exception chaining: Raising a clearer higher-level exception while preserving the original cause with 'from exc'. Quarantine: Separating bad records from
valid processing with evidence rather than silently dropping them. Fail fast: Stop at the earliest point where continuing would make the result unsafe.
VISUAL/SOURCE ROUTE: Book-led; Python Errors and Exceptions is authoritative.
After watching/opening: return to this lesson and reproduce the worked example from your own file/query/report. Save course-task evidence, not a screenshot of the
Circuit-breaker panel: catch only errors you can handle, translate them with useful context, clean up resources, and stop publication when the failure
threatens correctness. A blanket except that continues is a broken safety circuit.
Teacher demonstration - do this once with me, then close the example before your fresh task.
Create require_columns() that raises ValueError with the exact missing list.
Wrap file loading only to add path/business context; preserve FileNotFoundError or chain a meaningful error.
Do not catch an exception unless you can recover or add useful context.
Treat failed key uniqueness/reconciliation as a business-quality blocker even if no Python exception happened.
Write final business output only after critical validation returns PASS.
8. What you should see / be able to say
A workflow that either publishes trusted output or stops/quarantines with clear evidence.
Failure paths are designed rather than accidentally hidden by broad catches. Professional upgrade: Operational scripts need safe failure, evidence and
rerunability; these habits transfer directly to scheduled pipelines.
1. except Exception: pass. | 2. Logging SUCCESS in finally even after failure. | 3. Dropping malformed rows without count/evidence. | 4. Writing
output before checks then raising afterwards.
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
Remove broad handlers. Let the original error surface. Add one specific handler only where you can improve the message or recover safely. Save the
12. Now you do a small version alone
Fresh case: inject missing file, missing column, duplicate master key and malformed numeric record; define stop/quarantine behavior for each.
Every failure message identifies file/rule/context; critical failure prevents final release file.
14. Teach it back in your own words
Explain why 'the script did not crash' can still be a failed automation run.
Attempt first. Changed retry introduces a new bad record and requires quarantine or fail with evidence.
Failure matrix + code + captured messages + withheld-output proof + explain-back. After saving evidence, continue to PYA9.
When an unattended job runs at 6 AM, you need evidence of what files it found, what it transformed, which checks passed and why output
was released or withheld. Print statements alone are a poor operational history.
Configure meaningful logging and create machine-readable validation records containing check name, status, observed value and
expectation/rule. Separate technical completion from business validation.
PYA8 defensive failure handling and basic dictionaries/JSON.
5. New words before we use them
Logger: Named logging object used to emit records at levels such as INFO, WARNING and ERROR. Validation record: Structured result of one
business/data-quality check. Observability: Evidence that helps operators understand what a run did and where/why it failed.
VISUAL/SOURCE ROUTE: Corey Schafer Logging Basics - full targeted sections on levels, file output and formatting.
After watching/opening: return to this lesson and reproduce the worked example from your own file/query/report. Save course-task evidence, not a screenshot of the
Flight recorder plus checklist: logs explain what the run did and validation records state PASS/FAIL with observed values. Together they make
failures diagnosable and allow the release gate to block output for objective reasons.
Teacher demonstration - do this once with me, then close the example before your fresh task.
Configure logging with timestamp, level and message. Use a named logger.
Log meaningful checkpoints: run_start, files_discovered, rows_loaded, validation_complete, output_written/withheld.
Build checks as dictionaries with check, status, observed and rule/expected fields.
If a key-uniqueness or reconciliation check fails, log WARNING/ERROR and withhold final output even if the Python process technically
Write validation_results.json separately from the log so another process/person can inspect checks structurally.
8. What you should see / be able to say
One log that reconstructs the run story plus a machine-readable validation file that explains PASS/FAIL.
Operational events and business trust checks are both recorded; neither substitutes for the other. Professional upgrade: Logging levels should tell the run
story while structured validation supports automated gating/reporting. Do not log secrets or unnecessary row-level data.
1. Logging every row/line and hiding important events in noise. | 2. INFO says success although a critical validation failed. | 3. Validation file
contains only PASS/FAIL with no observed/rule values. | 4. Secrets or raw sensitive payloads written into logs.
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
List the 5-7 events a second analyst would need during incident recovery. Log only those plus warnings/errors; add structured checks for business
trust. Save the genuine attempt before review.
12. Now you do a small version alone
Fresh case: add logging and JSON validation to a customer enrichment run with duplicate-key, unmatched-key and total reconciliation checks.
Log has stage sequence; validation JSON has check/status/observed/rule; failed critical check blocks output.
14. Teach it back in your own words
Explain the difference between 'script finished' and 'business validation passed'.
Attempt first. Changed retry adds a new validation rule without rewriting logging setup.
run.log + validation_results.json + withheld-output failure proof + explain-back. After saving evidence, continue to PYA10.
A weekly report is not automated merely because Python creates the file. The workflow must run from a clean start, be safe to rerun and
avoid duplicating business rows or mutating raw inputs.
Orchestrate the module into one callable reporting workflow; externalize run period/paths; gate output on validation; make unchanged reruns
5. New words before we use them
Idempotent-ish rerun: For this analyst context, rerunning the same approved inputs/config should not duplicate underlying business results or corrupt raw
data. Orchestration: Coordinating smaller load/transform/validate/write functions in the required order. Release gate: A check that prevents publishing when
VISUAL/SOURCE ROUTE: Book-led; logging and pathlib references support the workflow. Scheduling UI is optional and environment-specific.
After watching/opening: return to this lesson and reproduce the worked example from your own file/query/report. Save course-task evidence, not a screenshot of the
Scheduled train with idempotent destination: config chooses the period, discovery/transform/validate stages run in order, publish occurs only on
PASS, and repeating the same approved run replaces/reproduces the defined output instead of duplicating business rows.
Teacher demonstration - do this once with me, then close the example before your fresh task.
Config supplies input_dir, customer_master, reporting_period and output_dir.
run_weekly discovers approved files, loads/cleans data and validates master-key assumptions before merge.
Use merge(..., validate='many_to_one') when that cardinality is the contract; surface unmatched keys.
Run structured checks. If any critical check is FAIL, raise/withhold final report.
Write report/log/validation/manifest to a defined run folder or deterministic filenames. Run twice on unchanged inputs and compare row
8. What you should see / be able to say
One callable weekly workflow that can be run manually from clean state and rerun without duplicate business data.
The orchestration calls tested components and final publishing depends on explicit trust checks. Professional upgrade: Use Windows Task Scheduler, cron or
an orchestration platform only after the script has deterministic manual-run and rerun behavior. Scheduling is deployment, not correctness.
1. Scheduling before a clean manual run passes. | 2. Appending to last week's output blindly. | 3. Changing raw source files during cleaning. | 4.
Duplicating transformation logic inside the scheduler entry point.
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
Disable scheduling. Run manually from a clean folder. Prove first run, second unchanged run, and one validation-failure run before automating
cadence. Save the genuine attempt before review.
12. Now you do a small version alone
Fresh case: build a weekly support-performance workflow whose reporting period changes only in config and whose rerun replaces/reproduces the
Second unchanged run does not duplicate business rows; raw inputs unchanged; every stage traceable; critical validation gates publish.
14. Teach it back in your own words
Explain why 'Task Scheduler launched Python' is not enough to call a reporting workflow reliable.
Attempt first. Changed retry switches reporting period through config only.
Callable workflow + config + two-run comparison + failure-gate proof + explain-back. After saving evidence, continue to PYA11.
A report that worked on your laptop is not reproducible if nobody knows which files, configuration, Python/pandas versions or dependency
Externalize configuration, use a project virtual environment, capture dependencies/versions and create a run manifest with inputs, row counts,
5. New words before we use them
Virtual environment: Isolated Python environment for a project with its own installed packages. Dependency capture: Recording package
requirements/versions needed to recreate the project environment. Run manifest: Machine-readable record of one run's configuration, inputs, versions,
VISUAL/SOURCE ROUTE: Optional visual: Corey Schafer VENV on Windows; current Python 3.14 venv docs control commands.
After watching/opening: return to this lesson and reproduce the worked example from your own file/query/report. Save course-task evidence, not a screenshot of the
Reproducibility recipe: code + config + isolated environment + exact inputs + dependency/version record + validation results + output hash/path form
a run manifest that another analyst can use to reconstruct what produced the report.
Teacher demonstration - do this once with me, then close the example before your fresh task.
Move file paths/reporting period into config.json; transformation code reads config rather than embedding personal paths.
Create a project venv using the current Python 3.14 venv workflow on the learner machine; install only needed dependencies.
Capture Python, pandas and other key dependency versions in a reproducible form appropriate to the project/team.
At each run, record UTC timestamp, config identifier, exact input file names/sizes/hashes where practical, rows, validation results and output
Move the project to a different parent folder or start a clean process and reproduce using configuration/root-path change only.
8. What you should see / be able to say
Another analyst can identify and recreate the run inputs/environment and reproduce the same business output within defined controls.
The result is tied to explicit code/config/environment/input evidence rather than personal laptop state. Professional upgrade: Reproducibility is the bridge from
analyst automation to engineering operations, incident recovery and later orchestration/CI practices.
1. requirements file never updated after package change. | 2. Absolute personal paths embedded in code. | 3. Manifest records output but not
inputs/config/version. | 4. Calling a notebook reproducible because it was saved.
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
Ask what a second machine needs: code, config, environment, inputs and run evidence. Add the first missing item before changing business logic.
Save the genuine attempt before review.
12. Now you do a small version alone
Fresh case: package the weekly reporting workflow into project folders with config.json, requirements/dependency capture, outputs/logs and manifest.
Reproduce from a changed root directory.
Config separate; versions recorded; exact inputs identifiable; second clean process/root reproduces row/total/output controls.
14. Teach it back in your own words
Explain reproducibility as the ability to answer 'what exactly produced this result and can we recreate it?'
Attempt first. Changed retry moves the project root and modifies period in config only.
Project tree + config + venv/dependency evidence + run manifest + clean reproduction proof + explain-back. After saving evidence, complete the module
mastery checklist and follow the Gate A / completion route.
Use after the first pass; this does not replace running the automation
PYA1 Does it run from a clean process? | PYA2 Are function contracts visible/testable? | PYA3 Are dtypes/bad records/reconciliations
explicit? | PYA4 Are expected files, lineage and schema drift controlled? | PYA5 Does exported Excel round-trip reconcile? | PYA6 What
does one flattened JSON row mean? | PYA7 Can API failure/hang/HTTP error be distinguished from valid JSON? | PYA8 Does a critical
failure stop release safely? | PYA9 Can logs + validation reconstruct trust? | PYA10 Can the same inputs rerun without duplicate
business data? | PYA11 Can another machine/process identify and recreate the exact run?
Hidden notebook state; hard-coded personal paths; silent
coercion; uncontrolled file glob; lost lineage; output not re-read;
wrong nested grain; API without timeout/status check; broad
swallowed exception; validation failure ignored; rerun duplicates;
Clean process -> expected files -> schema/types -> transform ->
withhold/release -> rerun -> manifest. Fix the first broken
contract, not the last visible symptom.
C2-05 intentionally introduces engineering habits such as deterministic ingestion, data-quality gates, observability, rerun safety and
reproducibility. Those skills help C2B/C3, but taking C2-05 itself is not required for the direct fast route.

C2-05 Protected Practice Review
OPEN ONLY AFTER THE MATCHING GENUINE ATTEMPT
Course 2A - C2-05 Protected Learning
Page 1
HOW TO USE
Compare contracts and evidence, not exact code text. Preserve the original attempt. If weak, close this review, repair the specific
competency and solve the changed retry without reopening it.
CRITICAL ANTI-CHEAT RULE
A reviewed/corrected script is not mastery. Clean-start execution, validation, failure handling and changed transfer are the evidence.
Never use this review during Gate A/B/C.
MODULE SAFETY SIGNALS
No hidden notebook state; no uncontrolled file glob; no silent dtype coercion; no lost lineage; no unverified Excel output; no wrong
JSON grain; no API without timeout/status handling; no swallowed critical error; no publish after failed validation; no duplicate rerun; no
run without reproducibility evidence.

2. Expected reasoning path
Declare expected file set before discovery; malformed file is rejected/quarantined with evidence rather than silently coerced.
Validate customer master uniqueness before merge. C005 duplicate is a critical block; do not drop one row merely to make
the merge run.
Preserve C999 as unmatched evidence. A left merge with indicator/cardinality checks is safer than hiding the exception.
Reconcile 90 approved order rows and 115,976.44 sales before and after enrichment. A naive duplicate-key merge would
create 96 rows and 122,135.78 sales.
Logs/validation explain the block; final output is written only after critical PASS. Re-run the same approved inputs and prove
no duplicate business result.
3. Critical failures
• Uncontrolled glob includes the malformed file.
• to_datetime/to_numeric coercion silently discards the bad row without a documented decision.
• Duplicate C005 is silently dropped or many-to-many merge is accepted.
• C999 disappears in an inner merge.
• Output is published before row/sales/key checks pass.
• Second run appends duplicate business rows.
• No manifest of Python/pandas, inputs, checks and output.
